key_claims: Mice fed a high-fat diet, particularly at 12 months of age, showed reduced gut microbiota diversity, depletion of Muribaculaceae, and decreased short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-linked functional signatures.

High-fat diet and age were associated with lower colonic butyrate levels, reduced expression of SCFA receptors (Ffar2, Ffar3) and tight-junction genes (Tjp1, Ocln), mislocalization of barrier proteins (ZO-1, occludin), higher serum LPS and inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α), and hippocampal-dependent cognitive and locomotor deficits.

Sodium butyrate supplementation in an intervention setting restored SCFA receptor and tight-junction expression, improved barrier integrity markers, lowered systemic cytokines, and rescued behavioral performance in mice.
limitations: The study was conducted in a mouse model, so the observed physiological and behavioral findings may not directly translate to humans.
The research relies on specific preclinical markers and intervention protocols that require further clinical validation in human populations.
what_not_to_say: Do not claim that sodium butyrate or Muribaculaceae depletion directly causes or cures cognitive decline or intestinal disorders in humans.
Do not state that these findings apply to human dietary interventions without further clinical trial evidence.
